questions.q: What is the most important part of the capstone write-up for demonstrating judgment, according to this lesson?
options: A complete list of every metric the service exposes
One real decision you made and the trade-off behind it, such as why you chose a particular alert threshold
A full product specification of what the service does
A list of every tool you considered but didn't use
questions.explain: Describing one real decision and its trade-off is what distinguishes genuine design judgment from simply having followed a checklist — that's the part interviewers actually remember.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend including an honest note on what you'd still add to the project?
options: Because it's required for a passing grade
Because admitting scope limits is a sign of maturity, not a weakness to hide
Because it replaces the need for an architecture sketch
Because unfinished projects are preferred over finished ones
questions.explain: The lesson frames being honest about what's missing or what you'd improve as a sign of maturity and self-awareness, which is viewed positively rather than as a shortcoming to conceal.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the architecture sketch in a capstone presentation?
options: To replace the dashboard entirely
To let the interviewer see the service, its dependency, and the data flow to dashboard and alerts in one glance, doing more work than paragraphs of description
To list every line of code in the project
It's purely decorative and has no functional purpose
questions.explain: A simple block diagram communicates the overall structure (service, dependency, data flow, dashboard, alerts) far faster than a verbal description, and is recommended to lead with in an interview.

questions.q: This lesson suggests structuring a verbal project walkthrough the same way as which other course artifact?
options: A runbook
An alert rule
A blameless postmortem
A status page update
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly draws the parallel: structure the walkthrough like a postmortem — what it does, what was measured and why, one trade-off, and what's next.

questions.q: What is the central point of having a capstone project at all, as summarized in this lesson?
options: To learn an entirely new set of tools not covered elsewhere in the course
To prove you can put everything from the course together on your own, without a script to follow, rather than to teach new material
To replicate the Northbridge Retail incident exactly
To memorize every PromQL function covered in Chapter 4
questions.explain: The capstone's purpose is synthesis and independent application of everything already taught — golden signals, the tooling, logging/tracing, and incident discipline — on a project of the student's own, not new content.
